questions.problem:
For the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ you're given the following data:

$$
f(-7)=2\sqrt{3},\,{f}^{′}(-7)=\sqrt{3},\,g(-7)=5\sqrt{3}\,{g}^{′}(-7)=-4\sqrt{3}
$$

Compute $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))$ at $x=-7.$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the product rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))=f(x){g}^{′}(x)+g(x){f}^{′}(x).
$$

At the point where $x=-7,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))|}_{x=-7} & =f(-7){g}^{′}(-7)+g(-7){f}^{′}(-7) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\cdot (-4\sqrt{3})+5\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)+p(x))={f}^{′}(x)+{p}^{′}(x).

$$

questions.problem:
For the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ you're given the following data:

$$
f(4)=-2,\,{f}^{′}(4)=4,\,g(4)=1,\,{g}^{′}(4)=0
$$

If $h(x)=\frac{2-3f(x)}{g(x)+1},$ compute ${h}^{′}(4).$
questions.worked_solution:
The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=2-3f(x)$ and $v=g(x)+1.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3{f}^{′}(x)\cdot (g(x)+1)-(2-3f(x))\cdot {g}^{′}(x)}{{(g(x)+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=4,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(4) & =\frac{-3{f}^{′}(4)\cdot (g(4)+1)-(2-3f(4))\cdot {g}^{′}(4)}{{(g(4)+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3\cdot 4\cdot (1+1)-(2-3\cdot (-2))\cdot 0}{{(1+1)}^{2}} \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

${h}^{′}(2)=$

Explanation:

The product rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(uv)=u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=-2f(x)-3$ and $v=g(x)+1.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-2{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={g}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting into the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =-2{f}^{′}(x)(g(x)+1)+(-2f(x)-3){g}^{′}(x).\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=2$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(2) & =-2{f}^{′}(2)(g(2)+1)+(-2f(2)-3){g}^{′}(2) \\  & =-2(2)(-3+1)+(-2(4)-3)(5) \\  & =-4(-2)+(-8-3)\cdot 5 \\  & =8+(-11)(5) \\  & =8-55 \\  & =-47.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For the functions $p(x)$ and $q(x),$ you're given the following data:

$$
p(10)=-1,\,{p}^{′}(10)=-2,\,q(10)=2,\,{q}^{′}(10)=1
$$

If $z(x)=(2p(x)+q(x))(2-p(x))$, compute ${z}^{′}(10).$
questions.worked_solution:
The product rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(uv)=u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let $u=2p(x)+q(x)$ and $v=2-p(x).$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-{p}^{′}(x).
$$

Substituting this into the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}(x) & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(2p(x)+q(x))(-{p}^{′}(x))+(2-p(x))(2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x)) \\  & =-{p}^{′}(x)(2p(x)+q(x))+(2{p}^{′}(x)+{q}^{′}(x))(2-p(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=10,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{′}(10) & =-{p}^{′}(10)(2p(10)+q(10))+(2{p}^{′}(10)+{q}^{′}(10))(2-p(10)) \\  & =-(-2)(2(-1)+2)+(2(-2)+1)(2-(-1)) \\  & =2(-2+2)-3(2+1) \\  & =0-9 \\  & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

| $t$ | $h(t)$ | $z(t)$ | ${h}^{′}(t)$ | ${z}^{′}(t)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $2$ | $5$ | $8$ | $-3$ | $4$ |

If $f(t)=\frac{1-h(t)}{z(t)},$ compute ${f}^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The quotient rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{u}{v})=\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}}.
$$

Let $u=1-h(t)$ and $v=z(t).$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-{h}^{′}(t)\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={z}^{′}(t).
$$

Substituting this into the quotient rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{{u}^{′}v-u{v}^{′}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-{h}^{′}(t))\cdot z(t)-(1-h(t))\cdot {z}^{′}(t)}{(z(t))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-z(t){h}^{′}(t)-{z}^{′}(t)(1-h(t))}{{z}^{2}(t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At $t=2,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{-z(2){h}^{′}(2)-{z}^{′}(2)(1-h(2))}{{z}^{2}(2)} \\  & =\frac{-8\cdot (-3)-4\cdot (1-5)}{{8}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{24+16}{64} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
The values of functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=0$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $-2$ | $0$ |

Compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\big(f(x)g(x)\big)$ at $x=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the product rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\big(f(x)g(x)\big) = f(x)g'(x)+f'(x)g(x).
$$

At the point where $x=0$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(f(x)g(x))|}_{x=0} & =f(0){g}^{′}(0)+{f}^{′}(0)g(0) \\  & =1\cdot 0+3\cdot (-2) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Quotient Given the Necessary Data
canonical_examples.problem:
The values of functions $h(x)$ and $z(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=-1$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | $h(x)$ | $z(x)$ | $h'(x)$ | $z'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $-4$ | $2$ | $6$ | $3$ |

Compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{h(x)}{z(x)}\right)$ at $x=-1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{h(x)}{z(x)}\right) = \dfrac{h'(x)z(x)-h(x)z'(x)}{(z(x))^2}.
$$

At the point where $x=-1$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{h(x)}{z(x)})|}_{x=-1} & =\frac{{h}^{′}(-1)z(-1)-h(-1){z}^{′}(-1)}{(z(-1))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot 3}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{24}{4} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of a Linear Combination of Functions Given the Necessary Data
canonical_examples.problem:
The values of functions $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ and their derivatives at $x=-3$ are given in the table below.

| $x$ | $p(x)$ | $q(x)$ | $p'(x)$ | $q'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-3$ | $1$ | $8$ | $0$ | $-2$ |

Compute $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\big( p(x) + 5q(x) \big)$ at $x=-3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the sum and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( p(x) + 5q(x) \right) = p'(x) + 5q'(x).
$$

At the point where $x=-3$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(p(x)+5q(x))|}_{x=-3} & ={p}^{′}(-3)+5{q}^{′}(-3) \\  & =0+5\cdot (-2) \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Derivative of the Product or Quotient of a Composition of Functions Given the Necessary Data
canonical_examples.problem:
For the functions $f(x)$ and $g(x),$ we have

$$
f(1)=2, \quad f'(1)=2, \quad g(1)=-1, \quad g'(1)=3.
$$

If  $h(x) = \left( f(x)-1 \right)\left(2g(x)+1\right),$  compute  $h'(1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The product rule states that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\Big(uv\Big) = u \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} +v \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm d x}.
$$

Let $u=f(x)-1$ and $v=2g(x)+1.$ Differentiating each, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = f'(x) \qquad  \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x} = 2g'(x).
$$

Substituting this into the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(x) & =u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}+v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =(f(x)-1)\cdot 2{g}^{′}(x)+(2g(x)+1)\cdot {f}^{′}(x) \\  & =2{g}^{′}(x)(f(x)-1)+{f}^{′}(x)(2g(x)+1).\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=1$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(1) & =2{g}^{′}(1)(f(1)-1)+{f}^{′}(1)(2g(1)+1) \\  & =2\cdot 3\cdot (2-1)+2\cdot (2\cdot (-1)+1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
